item.title: FREE ->->-> Luce & Raifa: Games and decisions
item.description: This review will be different. It will be live, like programming in Lisp. I will add quotes I found notable, useful, or remember-worthy here. Not all, mind, just the ones I think deserve a space in a reflective review. That’s to say, something to remind me of the key, useful ideas of the book when I re-read this review some time later. This is why the book has no rating, but a ’live review’ symbol (->->->).

item.title: Why read fiction?
item.description: But first, let’s clear definitional problems. What’s fiction? What kind of fiction? I specifically avoid the term Literature mainly because of its other meanings and didn’t want the title to have scientific or strictly academic connotations. But let me also be clear from the start: I don’t consider it art if it’s not literature, and most of the modern fiction doesn’t qualify. So when I ask that question, I have originally or truly meant: is there value to be had in reading great works of literature?

item.title: The antifragile mindset
item.description: When we’re young and naive, every minor unfavorable event that happens to us makes us far too sad, angry, or otherwise disappointed than we should objectively have been. I remember my first break-up and how seriously it had impacted me then. If I had been wiser, and someone with the knowledge and experience found in this essay would have told me then the secret to dealing with minor shocks, I’d have probably wasted less time and energy moping and pitying myself, and would have certainly dedicated myself to more uplifting, worthier projects.

item.title: ☆☆★★★★★★★★ Trollope: The Framley Parsonage
item.description: Summary: A deep psychological study of control, power, and Trans-Per. Pages: 700+ Rating: 8/10 Here I am again, surprising my ADHD self with yet another thick novel under the belt, and that too without a serious disruption of my daily schedule. How is it possible? If someone had told me it was easily possible, due to how constancy (I will define this soon) works, I would have yawned and never believed them; this is like the feeling of becoming a parent.

item.title: ☆☆☆★★★★★★★ Trollope: He knew he was right
item.description: TLDR in summary: Better than expected. Pages: 800+ Rating: 7/10 Finally! I started HKHWR in early 2019, but life happened and back it went into my library. In the meantime, seven years passed and I became a rather sophisticated reader. And since I don’t like loose ends, I decided to finish it, once and for all. I say that phrase because back in 2019, I read all the way near the second half, but somehow I couldn’t go further.

item.title: Why keep writing
item.description: Francis Bacon’s chew-and-digest category of books can, upon reflection, be also extended to essays and shorter writings. If the writing is good, length doesn’t matter. It was this idea that came up from the bottom of my subconscious well just now, but I’m not sure what else will turn up, so let’s go rummaging. For starters, every now and then I happen to chance upon a very well-written writing, either an essay or a blog post, or even a paragraph (such as the ones found on Amazon when someone takes the trouble and time to review a book for our benefit–for which I am grateful), that I find either useful, or interesting, or mind-bending, even hilarious, or simply well-written, etc.

item.title: ☆☆☆★★★★★★★ Trollope: The Eustace Diamonds
item.description: Rating: 7/10 On a whim, I had bought several Penguin Classics editions of Anthony Trollope’s novels, but several years ago when I picked one randomly, I had chanced upon ‘He knew he was right’, and I confess that at roughly 800+ pages, it seemed kind of slow-moving. As you probably know, I (am proud to) have ADHD, so it’s really not easy to do anything– let alone read. But as those who know how ADHD really functions already realize, once we’re certain our energy is not wasted, we pour it all in–what is called hyperfocus in certain circles.

item.title: ☆☆☆★★★★★★★ Matthew Lewis: The Monk
item.description: Rating: 7/10 Despite the fact that Lewis’s work has been unfairly villified by readers with substandard comprehension and critical thinking skills, one day when I finally regained access to my Penguin Classics library (it’s a long story and I don’t care to mention it), I decided it was time I read it. As soon as I read the introduction, I realized the book and its author were presented in an overly negative light–perhaps unintentionally or even unconsciously.

item.title: ☆★★★★★★★★★ Lermontov: A Hero of Our Time
item.description: Rating: 9/10 What a fantastic find! Lermontov is a poet at heart and his prose shows it. The story was unputdownable, but at the same time, made me imagine, think, and even learn some real-world wisdom. Though he claimed that he was not using himself in the protagonist, he was subtly using the protagonist to express his own opinions. I know this because some of the things his protagonist was saying or thinking were almost similar to some ideas I had been entertaining, ideas that you can’t have unless you think them over for a very long time, and in response to vagaries of the social environment.
